```{r}
#| echo: false
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(tidyverse))
options(width = 60, pillar.width = 60)
avo <- read_rds("../data/Avonet/AVONET1_BirdLife.rds")
big <- function(x){ format(round(x), big.mark = ",") }

parrot_fam1 <- avo[which(avo$Family1 == "Psittacidae"), ]
parrot_fam2 <- avo |> filter(Family1 == "Psittacidae")
forest_parrots <- avo |> filter(Family1 == "Psittacidae" & Habitat == "Forest")
p_or_c <- avo |> filter(Family1 %in% c("Psittacidae", "Cacatuidae"))
forest_p_or_c <- avo |>
  filter((Family1 == "Psittacidae" | Family1 == "Cacatuidae") & Habitat == "Forest")
no_parens <- avo |>
  filter(Family1 == "Psittacidae" | Family1 == "Cacatuidae" & Habitat == "Forest")
raptors_no_parens <- avo |>
  filter(Habitat == "Forest" & Trophic.Level == "Carnivore" &
         Family1 == "Accipitridae" | Family1 == "Falconidae")
raptors <- avo |> filter(Habitat == "Forest" & Trophic.Level == "Carnivore" &
                         Family1 %in% c("Accipitridae", "Falconidae"))
longest <- avo |> arrange(desc(Wing.Length)) |> slice(1)
beak_diff <- avo |>
  mutate(beak_length_difference = Beak.Length_Culmen - Beak.Length_Nares) |>
  arrange(desc(beak_length_difference))
avo_w_family_mass <- avo |> group_by(Family1) |> mutate(fam_mean_mass = mean(Mass))
avo_frac <- avo_w_family_mass |> mutate(frac = Mass / sum(Mass))
avo_frac_fixed <- avo_w_family_mass |> ungroup() |> mutate(frac = Mass / sum(Mass))
habitats <- avo |> group_by(Habitat) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_mass = mean(Mass)) |> arrange(desc(mean_mass))
biggest_in_fams <- avo |> group_by(Family1) |> slice_max(Mass, n = 1)
smallest_in_fams <- avo |> group_by(Family1) |> slice_min(Mass, n = 1)
```

# The tidyverse

## tidyverse {.smaller}

**A collection of R packages** built on a similar syntax.

**Designed to work together.**

**Very useful for data wrangling and data visualization.**

**Many people find them more intuitive than base R.**

::: {.notes}
One minute. Today is dplyr, the wrangling package. Next class is ggplot2, the
plotting package. Both load with library(tidyverse).
:::

## dplyr {.smaller}

**Used for data wrangling.**

**More readable than base R** (to most).

**The downside:** the syntax is still evolving.

**Designed for use with pipes:** `%>%` or `|>`

::: {.notes}
One minute. "Still evolving" is worth a sentence: answers on Stack Overflow from
a few years ago sometimes use functions that have since been renamed or retired.
`|>` is the pipe built into R since 4.1, and it's the one we use; `%>%` is the
older one from the magrittr package, and they'll see it in older code.
:::

## dplyr {.smaller}

dplyr functions:

| Step | |
|---|---|
| Take in | a data.frame (or tibble) |
| Do | something |
| Return | a data.frame (or tibble) |

This means that you can easily chain functions together with pipes!

```{r}
#| eval: false
data |>
  do_something() |>
  do_something_else()
```

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. Read the pipe aloud as "and then". A tibble is the tidyverse's
version of a data frame: it prints more tidily, and that's most of the
difference they will notice.
:::

## Tidyverse update! {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}

Does what dplyr does, but using Gen Z slang.

Use it on Assignment 2 for 1% extra credit.
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
![](figures/07_genzplyr_logo.png){width="85%"}
:::
::::

One minute, for fun. It's a real package by dplyr's own author, Hadley Wickham.
:::

# Getting set up

## Getting data {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

We'll work with the AVONET data again.

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
library(tidyverse)
avo <- read_rds("https://tinyurl.com/avonetbirddata")
```
:::

**Go ahead and load the data now.**

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. read_rds() reads R's own file format, which keeps the column types
exactly as they were saved, so there's nothing to check the way there was with
read.csv() in Lecture 4. The short link points at the .rds copy in the course
repository.
:::

# Operating on rows

## Operating on rows {.smaller}

We're going to start by talking about functions that operate on rows:

| Function | What it does |
|---|---|
| `filter()` | keeps the rows that meet a condition |
| `arrange()` | sorts the rows |
| `distinct()` | removes duplicate rows |

::: {.notes}
Thirty seconds.
:::

## Filtering data {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

**base R:**

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
parrot_fam1 <- avo[which(avo$Family1 == "Psittacidae"), ]
```
:::

**dplyr:**

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
parrot_fam2 <- avo |>
  filter(Family1 == "Psittacidae")
```
:::

**Try these now and see if you notice any differences.**

::: {.fragment}
**Check:** the same `r nrow(parrot_fam2)` rows. The row names differ: base R
keeps the originals (`r rownames(parrot_fam1)[1]`, `r rownames(parrot_fam1)[2]`,
...), `filter()` renumbers from 1.
:::

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. The base R line is last week's. The dplyr version doesn't repeat
avo$ and doesn't need which() or the trailing comma, and those are the three
things students got wrong most often last week.
:::

## Filtering on multiple columns {.smaller}

In R we can use:

| | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `&` (AND) | multiple conditions have to be met |
| <code>&#124;</code> (OR, vertical line) | either condition can be met |

This can be used to make our filtering more complex.

(Note that my favorite Star Wars media is thus "&|".)

::: {.notes}
One minute. "Andor", for anyone who missed it. The vertical line is above the
Enter key on most keyboards, with Shift.
:::

## Filtering on multiple columns: & {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
forest_parrots1 <- avo[which(avo$Family1 == "Psittacidae" &
                             avo$Habitat == "Forest"), ]

forest_parrots2 <- avo |>
  filter(Family1 == "Psittacidae" &
           Habitat == "Forest")

forest_parrots3 <- avo |>
  filter(Family1 == "Psittacidae") |>
  filter(Habitat == "Forest")
```
:::

**Are these all equivalent? Try them and find out.**

::: {.fragment}
**Check:** yes, all three have `r nrow(forest_parrots)` rows (only the row names
differ in the base R one).
:::

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. Two filters in a row is the same as one filter with &, which is
the pipe doing what it promises: each step takes the output of the last.
:::

## Filtering on multiple columns: & {.smaller}

**Your turn!**

Filter the `avo` dataset to only include:

A single order (of your choice)

A single trophic level

::: {.notes}
Four minutes. Students will need the spellings: unique(avo$Order1) and
unique(avo$Trophic.Level) list them, and both lines are in
R_scripts/Lecture_07_examples.R.
:::

## Filtering on multiple columns: | {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
parrots_or_cockatoos <- avo |>
  filter(Family1 == "Psittacidae" |
           Family1 == "Cacatuidae")
```
:::

Alternative using `%in%` and a vector:

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
parrots_or_cockatoos2 <- avo |>
  filter(Family1 %in% c("Psittacidae", "Cacatuidae"))
```
:::

**Try running these now.**

::: {.fragment}
**Check:** `r nrow(p_or_c)` rows each.
:::

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. %in% is the one to remember: with five families, the | version is
five lines and the %in% version is still one.
:::

## Filtering on multiple columns: & and | {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

Let's say we wanted parrots OR cockatoos, but only the ones that live in
forests. We need to make our filter more complex: we can combine `&`, `|`, and
`()` to achieve this.

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
forest_p_or_c <- avo |>
  filter((Family1 == "Psittacidae" | Family1 == "Cacatuidae") &
           Habitat == "Forest")
table(forest_p_or_c$Habitat)
```
:::

**Try this now! Then delete the grouping parentheses and run it again. What
changed?**

::: {.fragment}
**Check:** `r nrow(forest_p_or_c)` rows, all forest. Without the parentheses,
`r nrow(no_parens)`, from `r length(table(no_parens$Habitat))` habitats: R does
`&` before `|`, so it reads "parrots anywhere, or forest cockatoos".
:::

::: {.notes}
Four minutes. Let them run both before clicking. The table() line is there so
the mistake is visible: with the parentheses there is one habitat, without them
there are six, from desert to woodland.

The rule: & is done before |, the way multiplication is done before addition.
Without parentheses, R reads A | B & C as A | (B & C), which here means every
parrot plus only the forest cockatoos. The habit worth teaching is to write the
parentheses whenever & and | appear together, so nobody (including you, later)
has to remember the rule.

Nothing errors. The only sign is a row count that is too big, which is why the
table() check is worth the extra line.
:::

## Filtering on multiple columns: & and | {.smaller}

**Your turn:**

**Make a version of the data that only contains forest carnivores in either the
family "Accipitridae" or "Falconidae".**

::: {.fragment}
**Check:** `r nrow(raptors)` rows: `r sum(raptors$Family1 == "Accipitridae")`
hawks and eagles, `r sum(raptors$Family1 == "Falconidae")` falcons. Got
`r nrow(raptors_no_parens)`? Check your parentheses.
:::

::: {.notes}
Four minutes. Three conditions, one of which is an OR: the same shape as the
last slide, so it practices the parentheses. Without them you get every falcon
in the dataset, whatever its habitat or diet. The %in% version is the tidiest
answer and needs no parentheses at all, which is worth pointing out.
:::

## Sorting your data {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

We can use `arrange()` to sort by a column.

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
avo_by_mass <- avo |>
  arrange(Mass)

avo_by_mass_dec <- avo |>
  arrange(-Mass)

avo_by_mass_dec2 <- avo |>
  arrange(desc(Mass))
```
:::

**Use this syntax to figure out which bird has the longest wings.**

::: {.fragment}
**Check:** the Andean condor, *`r longest$Species1`*, at `r longest$Wing.Length` mm.
:::

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. The minus sign only works on numbers; desc() works on text too,
which is why it's the one to use.
:::

## distinct {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

Used to remove duplicate rows:

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
avo_no_dupes <- avo |>
  distinct()
```
:::

Can also be used on particular fields, or combinations of fields:

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
avo_fams <- avo |>
  distinct(Family1)

family_trophic_levels <- avo |>
  distinct(Family1, Trophic.Level)
```
:::

**What do these two data frames contain?**

::: {.fragment}
**Check:** the `r nrow(distinct(avo, Family1))` families, and the
`r nrow(distinct(avo, Family1, Trophic.Level))` family and trophic level
combinations that occur. (`avo` has no duplicate rows: still
`r big(nrow(distinct(avo)))`.)
:::

::: {.notes}
Three minutes.
:::

# Operating on columns

## Operating on columns {.smaller}

There are also functions that operate on columns:

| Function | What it does |
|---|---|
| `mutate()` | makes new columns, or changes existing ones |
| `select()` | keeps (or drops) columns |
| `rename()` | renames columns |
| `relocate()` | moves columns |

::: {.notes}
Thirty seconds.
:::

## Mutate {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

Can be used to create new variables or modify existing ones. Let's create a
variable calculating the difference between the two beak length measures:

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
avo_w_beak_diff <- avo |>
  mutate(beak_length_difference =
           Beak.Length_Culmen - Beak.Length_Nares)
```
:::

**Which bird has the largest difference between these measurements?**

**Is this an error?**

::: {.fragment}
**Check:** a kiwi, *`r beak_diff$Species1[1]`*: a difference of
`r beak_diff$beak_length_difference[1]` mm.
:::

::: {.notes}
Four minutes. Culmen length is measured from the feathers at the base of the
beak, Nares from the nostril. All three top spots are kiwis. Not an error:
kiwis are the only birds with their nostrils at the tip of the beak, which is
how they smell for worms. A callback to the kiwi in Lecture 5.

Worth asking: what about the other end? Sort ascending and a few species have a
negative difference, a nostril further from the tip than the feathers. That one
is worth a second look in a real analysis.
:::

## Select {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

Selects fields to keep (or remove).

Keep only family, species, mass:

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
fsm <- avo |>
  select(Family1, Species1, Mass)
```
:::

Toss range size:

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
no_rangesize <- avo |>
  select(!Range.Size)
```
:::

**Try these out now.**

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. ! means "not", the same as in last week's !is.na().
:::

## Select {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

We can also use the `:` syntax to select multiple fields.

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
avo_tax <- avo |>
  select(Species1:Order1)
```
:::

**Try this and see if you understand what it did.**

**How would you remove Primary.Lifestyle, Range.Size and everything in
between?**

::: {.fragment}
**Check:** `select(!(Primary.Lifestyle:Range.Size))`, which leaves
`r ncol(select(avo, !(Primary.Lifestyle:Range.Size)))` of the
`r ncol(avo)` columns.
:::

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. Species1:Order1 means "from Species1 to Order1, in the order the
columns sit", so it keeps three columns. names(avo) shows the order.
:::

## Rename {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

**Let's say we wanted to remove the 1s from the taxonomic variables:**

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
avo_tax1 <- avo |>
  rename(Species = Species1,
         Family = Family1,
         Order = Order1)
```
:::

**Note that you can do this during a `select()` as well:**

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
avo_tax2 <- avo |>
  select(Species = Species1,
         Family = Family1,
         Order = Order1,
         Mass)
```
:::

**Try these both out. How do they differ?**

::: {.fragment}
**Check:** `rename()` keeps all `r ncol(avo)` columns; `select()` keeps only the
4 you name.
:::

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. The new name goes on the left, the same way as in mutate().
:::

## Relocate {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

Often easier to have important variables on the left-most columns.

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
avo_relocated <- avo |>
  relocate(Order1, Family1, Species1, Mass, Wing.Length)
```
:::

**Try this and look at the avo_relocated data frame.**

**Why are only some of the variables relocated?**

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. relocate() moves the columns you name to the front, in the order
you name them, and leaves everything else where it was, after them. Nothing is
dropped: that's the difference from select().
:::

# Grouping

## Grouping {.smaller}

You can "group" rows of data together. This allows you to create summary
statistics for those groups, and it is usually combined with another function
like `summarise()`.

Important functions:

| Function | What it does |
|---|---|
| `group_by()` | marks the groups |
| `ungroup()` | removes them |
| `summarise()` | one row per group |
| `slice_*()` | picks rows within each group |

::: {.notes}
One minute. summarise() and summarize() are the same function, so either
spelling works.
:::

## Using group_by() {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

Let's add in family level mean mass information:

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
avo_w_family_mass <- avo |>
  group_by(Family1) |>
  mutate(fam_mean_mass = mean(Mass))
```
:::

**Run this and see if the results make sense.**

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. Every row gets its own family's mean: all the Accipitridae rows
say `r big(avo_w_family_mass$fam_mean_mass[avo_w_family_mass$Family1 == "Accipitridae"][1])`
g. Still `r big(nrow(avo_w_family_mass))` rows. Remember this object: it comes
back in a few slides.
:::

## summarise {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

If we ONLY wanted the data at the family level, we can use `summarise()`:

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
family_mass <- avo |>
  group_by(Family1) |>
  summarise(Mean_Mass = mean(Mass))
```
:::

**Try this. How many columns and how many rows do you get back?**

**Why these?**

::: {.fragment}
**Check:** `r nrow(distinct(avo, Family1))` rows and 2 columns: one row per
family, and only the grouping column plus the one you made.
:::

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. The contrast with the last slide is the point: mutate() keeps
every row, summarise() collapses each group to one.
:::

## More than one statistic {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
avo |>
  group_by(Trophic.Level) |>
  summarise(n           = n(),
            mean_mass   = mean(Mass),
            median_mass = median(Mass))
```
:::

`n()` counts the rows in each group.

**Try this and inspect the output.**

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. Two things to draw out. There's a fifth row, NA: five species
have no trophic level, and group_by() keeps them as their own group. And the
scavenger mean and median are close, while every other group's mean is several
times its median: the long right tail from Lecture 5.
:::

## What went wrong? {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
avo |>
  group_by(Trophic.Level) |>
  summarise(mean_range = mean(Range.Size))
```
:::

**What do you notice about the output?**

**What happened and what should we do?**

::: {.fragment}
**Check:** NA for every group except scavengers.
`r sum(is.na(avo$Range.Size))` species have no range size, and one NA makes the
whole mean NA. The fix: `mean(Range.Size, na.rm = TRUE)`.
:::

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. The same na.rm from Lecture 4, now inside summarise(). The
scavengers come out fine only because none of the 20 is missing a range size.
:::

## Still grouped {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

**Remember this, from earlier?**

```{r}
#| eval: false
avo_w_family_mass <- avo |>
  group_by(Family1) |>
  mutate(fam_mean_mass = mean(Mass))
```

**Simple question. How many species are in the dataset?**

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
avo_w_family_mass |>
  summarise(total_species = n())
```
:::

**Try it. Is that what you expected?**

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. They know the answer: it has been 11,009 since Lecture 5. Getting
243 rows back instead of one number is unmistakably wrong, which is why this is
the right question to ask first. Let them sit with it: nothing in the line they
just typed mentions families.

For comparison, run the same thing on avo itself and get one row reading 11009.
Same verb, same argument, different answer; the only difference is which object
it was pointed at.
:::

## group_by() is sticky {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

Grouping stays attached to the data until you remove it.

**R does tell you:**

::: {.out}
```{r}
#| echo: false
cat(capture.output(print(avo_w_family_mass))[1:2], sep = "\n")
```
:::

**The fix:**

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
avo_w_family_mass |>
  ungroup() |>
  summarise(total_species = n())
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. group_by() doesn't do anything on its own. It attaches a label
saying "treat this as 243 separate tables from now on", and every verb
downstream obeys until something removes it. mutate() never removes it, which is
why the object is still carrying the label many slides later. summarise()
removes one level, which is why the summarise slide gave one row per family.

Do it live: print avo_w_family_mass, point at the Groups line, then print the
ungrouped version and show the line is gone. The lesson is bigger than
ungroup(): read the header R prints for you. Same habit as str() in Lecture 4.
:::

## The quiet version {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

Let's calculate the fraction of total mass represented by each species:

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
avo_frac <- avo_w_family_mass |>
  mutate(frac = Mass / sum(Mass))
```
:::

`r big(nrow(avo_frac))` rows. Right shape. Looks fine.

::: {.out}
```{r}
#| echo: false
avo_frac |> ungroup() |> filter(Family1 == "Struthionidae") |>
  select(Species1, Mass, frac) |> as.data.frame()
```
:::

Half of all bird mass is one ostrich?

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
sum(avo_frac$frac)
```
:::

**What happened?**

::: {.fragment}
**Check:** `r sum(avo_frac$frac)`, not 1.
:::

::: {.notes}
Three minutes, and the important slide of the three. "Still grouped" failed
loudly, with the wrong number of rows. This one returns exactly the right number
of rows, with a plausible-looking column, and is completely wrong.

sum(Mass) inside a grouped data frame is the family total, not the dataset
total. There are two ostrich species with identical masses, so each is half of
its family. The fractions sum to 1 within every family, so across 243 families
they sum to 243. With ungroup() first, the ostrich comes out at
`r sprintf("%.4f", max(avo_frac_fixed$frac))`, and the column sums to 1.

Tie it back: this is the same failure as the y axis trap in Lecture 6. A result
that is correctly computed, correctly displayed, and answers a different
question than the one you asked. Nothing errors and nothing warns.
:::

## Your turn: Grouping {.smaller}

Using `group_by()` and `summarise()`:

1. How many species are in each Habitat?
2. Which habitat has the heaviest birds on average?
3. Add the number of species to your answer for 2. Does that change which
   habitat you would report?
4. Take `avo_w_family_mass` and find the single heaviest bird in the whole
   dataset. Watch the row count.

*(Watch out for NAs.)*

::: {.fragment}
**Check:** forest has the most species (`r big(sum(avo$Habitat %in% "Forest"))`);
marine birds are heaviest on average (`r big(habitats$mean_mass[1])` g, from
`r habitats$n[1]` species); question 4 gives
`r nrow(slice_max(avo_w_family_mass, Mass, n = 1))` rows until you `ungroup()`,
then the two ostriches.
:::

::: {.notes}
Eight minutes. The NA warning: there's an NA habitat group of
`r habitats$n[is.na(habitats$Habitat)]` species, which ranks third by mean mass.

Question 4 is the ungroup lesson, self-inflicted. The row count is one per
family plus ties: slice_max() keeps every row tied for the maximum, and plenty
of small families have species with identical masses. Ungrouped, the two
ostriches tie at 111,000 g.
:::

## Slice functions {.smaller}

These return a subset of data. They can be used to see just the first, the last,
or a random sample; they're useful for examining a subset of data (it speeds up
analyses), and for subsetting the biggest or smallest values.

| Function | Returns |
|---|---|
| `slice_head()` | the first rows |
| `slice_tail()` | the last rows |
| `slice_min()` | the rows with the smallest values |
| `slice_max()` | the rows with the largest values |
| `slice_sample()` | a random sample of rows |

::: {.notes}
One minute. All of them take n =, and on grouped data they work within each
group.
:::

## Slice functions {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

To get the largest bird species in each family:

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
biggest_in_fams <- avo |>
  group_by(Family1) |>
  slice_max(Mass, n = 1) |>
  select(Family1, Species1, Mass)
```
:::

**How would we modify this to get the smallest bird in each family?**

**Try it and see if you're right.**

::: {.fragment}
**Check:** `slice_min(Mass, n = 1)`. Expect more rows than families
(`r nrow(smallest_in_fams)`): ties are all kept.
:::

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. Ties come up again: biggest_in_fams has
`r nrow(biggest_in_fams)` rows for 243 families. Add with_ties = FALSE to get
exactly one per family.
:::

# Wrapping up

## Which tool, when {.smaller}

::: {.tiny-table}
| You want to | Use |
|---|---|
| keep the rows that match a condition | `filter()`, with `&`, <code>&#124;</code>, `%in%` |
| sort rows | `arrange()`, `desc()` |
| drop duplicate rows, or list the unique values | `distinct()` |
| make or change a column | `mutate()` |
| keep or drop columns | `select()`, with `!` and `:` |
| rename or reorder columns | `rename()`, `relocate()` |
| a statistic for every group | `group_by()` then `summarise()` |
| the biggest, smallest or first rows (per group) | `slice_max()`, `slice_min()`, `slice_head()` |
| stop working by group | `ungroup()`, and read the `# Groups:` line |
:::

::: {.notes}
The slide to photograph.
